steps.title: The metro and its four weeks
steps.say: An invented metro network: a core router, four aggregation routers, 44 sites (hubs on fibre or microwave, tail sites on microwave behind them) and 264 cells, with four weeks of counters every 15 minutes, vendor alarms and the configuration change log. Thirty-odd faults happened in those weeks and were all fixed before today. The anomaly detector and the traffic forecaster learn on three weeks and are scored on the last, each against a plain baseline; the history's alarms are correlated and the ranking is checked against the closed tickets.

steps.title: The network now
steps.say: The topology as the service holds it: sites placed on the map, each link coloured by its load in the last interval, standby microwave links dashed, protected sites (a hospital) marked. Then one cell, S10-B-L, over the last three days against its seasonal normal, with tomorrow's traffic forecast.

steps.title: A backhaul link degrades, a handover breaks
steps.say: The generator is told two things at 14:00 on a Monday. Half an hour later the microwave backhaul from hub S08 to its aggregation router loses half its capacity and starts dropping packets (rain on an E-band hop); every cell on S08 and its three tail sites sits behind it. An hour in, an engineer's change pushes a wrong neighbour table to cell S10-B-L, so handovers into it fail. Three hours of the network run: the service sees counters, vendor alarms and the change log, scores every cell and correlates every alarm as it lands.

steps.title: Hundreds of alarms, two incidents
steps.say: Correlation over the three hours: an alarm is explained by its element or anything upstream of it on today's routing, a handover alarm by its cell or the neighbour it fails towards. Hundreds of flapping alarms on 25 elements become one transport incident whose root is the degraded link, and the handover failures a second incident whose root is the cell that was changed. Each candidate root carries its evidence. A probe then reports into the same interval: two samples and an alarm accepted (the alarm joins the open incident), two samples refused with the reason.

steps.title: Forecast the overload, simulate the reroutes
steps.say: The traffic forecast rolled up to every link says the degraded link, already near its reduced capacity, will be well past it at the evening busy hour. The recommendation runs every subset of the possible reroutes behind it through the digital twin over the next 24 hours and checks each against the declared envelope: no link the plan touches above 80% (less a 5-point forecast margin), at most three elements changed, never move a protected site. The obvious move, rerouting everything that can be rerouted, is simulated too, and breaks the envelope. For the handover incident the recommendation is a rollback of the change.

steps.title: A second person approves a safe plan
steps.say: The engineer tries to propose the naive reroute and the policy engine refuses it. The recommended plan (two reroutes and the rollback) is proposed instead and re-checked on a fresh forecast. A proposal changes nothing: the engineer cannot approve it; the NOC manager does, the policy engine checks it once more, and the change orchestrator applies it from the next interval and logs every configuration change.

steps.title: Through the evening busy hour
steps.say: Six more hours run with the plan in place. The degraded link carries the traffic the twin said it would and stays inside the envelope through the busy hour, the standby path takes the two tail sites, and handover success on S10-B-L recovers. The link still drops packets for the sites left on it, so its incident stays open for a field visit. Then the audit trail, hash-chained.
